71.title: The messenger in the eastern place
71.hook: Maryam withdraws to a quiet place, and a messenger in the form of a man brings impossible news
71.howItsDone: Muslims read this scene in Surah Maryam and Surah Al 'Imran and honor Maryam as a woman of faith and purity; the phrase kun fa-yakun is often said when speaking of what only Allah can do.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nida'an khafiyya: an old man's whisper in the room of prayer, and a son named Yahya. Your line was he called in secret.

Maryam is grown now. She withdraws from her family to a place toward the east, the Qur'an says, and puts a screen between herself and them. Maybe to pray, maybe just to be quiet; the text doesn't say why, and it doesn't need to. Then, in that private place, a man is standing there, where a young woman went so that nobody would be. Her first words are not a scream. They're a name of God: I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you fear Him at all.
screen: `A PLACE TOWARD THE EAST.` → `A SCREEN, AND THEN A MAN.` → `I SEEK REFUGE IN THE MERCIFUL.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an tells us who he is before she knows: Allah sent Our Spirit to her, and he took the form of a man, well made. Muslims understand the Spirit here as the angel Jibril, the same messenger who, as this path will tell later, came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in a cave. Notice her first move: she reaches for ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful, the name inside the bismillah, from day one of this path. He answers gently: I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure son. Then Maryam asks the most honest question in the story. In Pickthall's translation: “How can I have a son when no mortal hath touched me, neither have I been unchaste?” She doesn't pretend to understand. She asks, and the Qur'an doesn't scold her for it. The answer is the one Zakariyya heard yesterday, word for word, for his impossible child: Thy Lord saith, “It is easy for Me.” Easy. Not for Maryam; it will be the hardest thing in her life. Easy for Him. In Surah Al 'Imran the same scene gives the reason: when Allah decides a thing, He only says to it, “Be! and it is.” In Arabic, kun fa-yakun. Christians know this scene as the Annunciation, and in the Gospel of Luke the angel is Gabriel. Muslims and Christians tell it differently in important ways, and both honor Maryam's courage in that room. Today the Qur'an gives a young woman alone with a question no human could answer, and an answer that doesn't explain; it just says who is able.
screen: `OUR SPIRIT, IN THE FORM OF A MAN.` · `HOW CAN I HAVE A SON?` · `IT IS EASY FOR ME.` · `KUN FA-YAKUN: BE, AND IT IS.` · then, large: `IT IS EASY FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: Let one question come that has no human answer: why this happened, what's next, how something impossible could ever work out. Don't answer it or push it away; ask it honestly, the way Maryam did, and sit next to it. If you pray, you can hand it to Allah with her words, I seek refuge in the Most Merciful; if you don't, just let the question stay open.
Kun fa-yakun, be, and it is: how Allah decides anything, the answer Maryam received to her honest question.
Your line: it is easy for him. Tomorrow, a palm tree in the desert. See you there.

72.title: The palm tree
72.hook: alone and in labor, Maryam holds on to a palm trunk, and is told to shake it, eat and drink
72.carry: shake the tree; eat; be glad
72.howItsDone: Muslims read the birth of Isa in Surah Maryam, and dates have their own place in Muslim life: the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have broken his fast with fresh dates.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kun fa-yakun: Jibril in the eastern place, and Maryam's honest question, how? The answer was your line: it is easy for Him.

No crowd, no inn, no star. The Qur'an gives us one young woman, far from home. She has gone off to a distant place, alone, and the labor pains begin. They drive her, the Qur'an says, to the trunk of a palm tree, and she holds on to it, the way a hand grabs for anything solid when pain comes in waves. And there Maryam, the woman honored above the women of the worlds, says something the Qur'an doesn't hide. She wishes she were dead.
screen: `FAR FROM HOME, ALONE.` → `SHE HOLDS THE PALM TRUNK.` → `SHE WISHES SHE WERE DEAD.`

segments.voice: Her words, in Pickthall's translation: “Oh, would that I had died ere this and had become a thing of naught, forgotten!” The Qur'an keeps that line. It lets one of the holiest women in its pages say the worst thing a person in pain can say, and it doesn't correct her. Then a voice calls to her from below. Commentators differ on who: some say the angel Jibril, some say the newborn child himself. Its first words: grieve not. Your Lord has put a stream beneath you. Then the part people remember: “And shake the trunk of the palm-tree toward thee, thou wilt cause ripe dates to fall upon thee.” Think about it. A woman who has just given birth can't shake a palm trunk; it hardly moves even for a strong man. Muslim teachers have drawn a lesson from that. The dates could simply have fallen. Instead she is asked to put her hand on the tree and do her small part, and Allah does the rest. Then three plain instructions: “So eat and drink and be consoled.” Eat. Drink. Be glad, or cool your eyes, as the Arabic puts it: let your eyes be at rest. Not a sermon. Food, water and comfort for a woman who has just been through labor. Christians tell Jesus's birth in their own way, in Bethlehem with a manger. The Qur'an's picture is this one: a palm tree, a stream and fresh dates.
screen: `WOULD THAT I HAD DIED ERE THIS.` · `GRIEVE NOT: A STREAM BENEATH YOU.` · `SHAKE THE TRUNK; THE DATES FALL.` · `EAT AND DRINK AND BE CONSOLED.` · then, large: `DO YOUR SMALL PART.`

segments.voice: If you have one nearby, take a date, or any piece of fruit, and look at it first: the color, the weight in your hand. Eat it slowly, letting each small bite sit on your tongue until the sweetness arrives, and think of Maryam under the tree, exhausted, being told: eat, drink, be glad. If you pray, you can say bismillah before the first bite and alhamdulillah after the last.
An-nakhlah, the date palm: the trunk Maryam held and shook in labor, until ripe dates fell for her to eat.
Your line: shake the tree; eat; be glad. Tomorrow, Maryam goes home with the baby. Day seventy-two, done.

73.title: The baby who spoke
73.hook: Maryam carries her baby home, says nothing to the accusations, and points to the cradle
73.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Isa speaking in the cradle in Surah Maryam, and his words, peace on me the day I was born, are recalled as a blessing on birth, death and rising.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an-nakhlah, the palm tree: Maryam in labor, a stream beneath her, dates falling. Your line was shake the tree; eat; be glad.

Maryam is walking home: unmarried, carrying a newborn, toward the people who know her family. There's no way to explain this. Any explanation she gives will sound like an excuse. Under the palm tree she was told what to do: if you meet anyone, say, I have vowed a fast to the Most Merciful, and I will not speak to anyone today. A fast of silence. So she walks into town, into the stares, and the voices start. O Maryam, you've done a terrible thing. Your father was a good man. Your mother was a decent woman. Maryam says nothing at all. She just points at the baby.
screen: `CARRYING HIM HOME.` → `A FAST OF SILENCE.` → `SHE POINTS AT THE BABY.`

segments.voice: They're baffled. In Pickthall's words: “How can we talk to one who is in the cradle, a young boy?” And then the baby speaks. “Lo! I am the slave of Allah. He hath given me the Scripture and hath appointed me a Prophet.” His first words aren't about himself as a wonder; they're about who he serves. Allah has made me blessed wherever I am, he goes on, told me to pray and give charity as long as I live, and to be kind to my mother. Not arrogant, not wretched. Then this line: “Peace on me the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I shall be raised alive!” If that sounds familiar, it should. A few verses earlier the Qur'an says almost the same words about Yahya, the son of nida'an khafiyya. Two prophets, two impossible births, one blessing. Notice who does the defending. Maryam doesn't argue or prove anything. She keeps her silence, and the truth speaks for her, from the cradle. One detail scholars discuss: the crowd calls her sister of Harun, of Aaron. Muslims understand this as a family or priestly connection, or a brother named Harun, not a claim that she was Musa's sister; a hadith in Sahih Muslim says people used to be named after earlier prophets and good people. Muslims count the cradle among Isa's miracles, and another surah names it too: he spoke to people in the cradle, and his first words cleared his mother's name.
screen: `HOW CAN WE TALK TO A BABY?` · `I AM THE SLAVE OF ALLAH.` · `PEACE ON ME THE DAY I WAS BORN.` · `SHE KEEPS SILENT; THE TRUTH SPEAKS.` · then, large: `LET THE TRUTH SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Keep a small fast of silence, as Maryam vowed to speak to no one that day: say nothing, and try to say nothing inside too. When your mind starts drafting a reply, an explanation, a defense, notice it, leave it unsent, and come back to the quiet. If you pray, you can leave your defense with Allah, as Maryam did.
Al-mahd, the cradle: where the infant Isa spoke his first words, I am a servant of Allah, while Maryam kept her silence.
Your line: let the truth speak. Tomorrow, who Isa is for Muslims. That's day seventy-three.

74.title: Isa, prophet of Allah
74.hook: Muslims honor Isa, son of Maryam, as a great prophet and messenger who healed by Allah's leave
74.tomorrow: the one who left in anger
74.howItsDone: Muslims honor Isa as one of the messengers of firm resolve, say 'peace be upon him' after his name, and read his story in Surahs Al 'Imran, Al-Ma'idah and Maryam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-mahd: the cradle where the baby spoke, and his mother's silence. Your line was let the truth speak.

Jesus is in the Qur'an. Not in a footnote: the name Isa comes up in surah after surah. His mother has a surah named after her. His birth, his first words and his miracles are all told. And when Muslims say his name, they add peace be upon him, as they do for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and the other prophets. After three days in the story of his birth, today steps back and asks: who is Isa, for Muslims?
screen: `JESUS IS IN THE QUR'AN.` → `IN SURAH AFTER SURAH.` → `WHO IS ISA, FOR MUSLIMS?`

segments.voice: The Qur'an gives him titles. He is al-Masih, the Messiah. He is called a word from Allah, and a spirit from Him. He was given a scripture, the Injil, the Gospel. One verse names him in a line with Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Muhammad, the five that tradition calls the messengers of firm resolve. Then his miracles. In Surah Al 'Imran, Isa lists them to his people: he shapes a bird from clay and breathes into it, and it becomes a bird. Then, in Pickthall's translation: “I heal him who was born blind, and the leper, and I raise the dead, by Allah's leave.” Listen for that last phrase, because it keeps coming back. By Allah's leave, by His permission; in Arabic, bi-idhni llah. It appears again and again when the Qur'an describes what Isa did. The miracles are real, the Qur'an says, and they are Allah's. Isa is the one they come through. That phrase holds the heart of how Muslims see him: a great and beloved prophet, born of a virgin mother, a healer, and a servant of Allah, not Allah himself. Here the two neighboring faiths part ways, so it's worth saying plainly who believes what. Christians believe Jesus is the Son of God, that he died on the cross and rose again. Muslims honor him as a prophet and messenger, and the Qur'an says he was not killed or crucified, though it was made to appear so, and that Allah raised him up. Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari speak of his return before the end. Both faiths honor him, and they understand him differently.
screen: `AL-MASIH: A WORD AND A SPIRIT.` · `THE BIRD OF CLAY, THE BLIND, THE DEAD.` · `BI-IDHNI LLAH: BY ALLAH'S LEAVE.` · `TWO FAITHS, TWO UNDERSTANDINGS.` · then, large: `A SERVANT OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who is sick, hurting or worn down right now, and picture them clearly. Choose words that would help them hear, not advice, something kind, like I'm thinking of you, you're not alone, or I'll bring dinner Thursday. If you pray, you can ask Allah to heal them, since the healing is His.
Isa. Jesus, son of Maryam: in Islam, the Messiah, a great prophet and messenger, who healed by Allah's leave.
Your line: by Allah's leave. That closes Maryam and Isa: a vow, a whisper, a messenger, a palm tree, a cradle, a healer. Tomorrow, a man who left in anger.

75.title: The one who left in anger
75.hook: Yunus gives up on his people, walks off in anger, boards a crowded ship, and is thrown into the sea
75.carry: walking away is also a choice
75.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Yunus in Surahs Yunus, Al-Anbiya, As-Saffat and Al-Qalam, and honor him as a prophet whose story teaches patience with people and turning back to Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isa, the Messiah and healer, who did it all by Allah's leave. That was your line. Today, a new prophet and a very different mood.

Ten explanations. Patience, and more patience. Every approach tried, and still nobody listens. Then the keys come off the hook, and the door closes, not slammed, just closed hard. A prophet named Yunus has been calling his people to Allah, and they won't have it. The Qur'an says, simply, he went off in anger. He heads for the sea and boards a ship. Anywhere but here. Then, out at sea, things go wrong.
screen: `THEY WON'T LISTEN.` → `HE WENT OFF IN ANGER.` → `HE BOARDS A SHIP.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an tells this story in pieces, across several surahs. Surah Al-Anbiya gives him a nickname, in Pickthall's words: “And (mention) Dhu'n-Nun, when he went off in anger.” Dhu n-Nun: the one of the fish. Surah As-Saffat has the ship: “When he fled unto the laden ship.” Fled. The Arabic word is the one for a runaway slave leaving his master; that's how the text names what he did. Commentators explain that Yunus left his people before Allah had given him leave to go. His frustration was understandable. His leaving was still a choice. Then trouble at sea. The Qur'an doesn't describe it; commentators say the ship was in danger and someone had to go over the side. They cast lots, and the lot falls on Yunus. He's thrown into the sea, and a great fish swallows him. The Qur'an says he was blameworthy at that moment, and doesn't pretend otherwise. And yet Yunus is still a prophet, honored by name: the tenth surah is called Yunus. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari to have said that no one should say he is better than Yunus, son of Matta. Another surah even tells the Prophet: be patient, and don't be like the companion of the fish. The lesson is gentle: Yunus is a warning and a beloved prophet at once, and the one who walked out is not written off. Jews and Christians know him too, as Jonah, from the Hebrew Bible. For now, leave him where the Qur'an leaves him today: in the dark, inside the fish.
screen: `DHU N-NUN: THE ONE OF THE FISH.` · `HE FLED UNTO THE LADEN SHIP.` · `THE LOTS FALL ON YUNUS.` · `NO ONE IS BETTER THAN YUNUS.` · then, large: `WALKING AWAY IS ALSO A CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Think of a place, a person, a job or a conversation you left in frustration; maybe you were right to be frustrated, and there's no need to argue that. Just notice the moment of leaving: what it felt like in your body, what you told yourself as you went, whether it was a choice or felt like the only option. If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you what you couldn't see then.
Dhu'n-Nun, the one of the fish: Yunus's name for the day he went off in anger and left his people behind.
Your line: walking away is also a choice. Tomorrow, what Yunus says in the dark. Day seventy-five.

76.title: Three darknesses
76.hook: in the night, in the sea, inside the fish, Yunus calls out: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong
76.tomorrow: the gourd and the saved city
76.howItsDone: Many Muslims say the prayer of Yunus, la ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu mina z-zalimin, in times of distress, sometimes repeating it many times, trusting the hadith that it is answered.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dhu'n-Nun: Yunus left his people in anger and ended up in the sea. Your line was walking away is also a choice.

Have you ever been somewhere truly dark? The kind where you hold your hand in front of your face and see nothing. Now stack it. It's night. Under the night, the sea. Under the sea, inside a great fish, a man. Early commentators called it three darknesses: the dark of the night, the dark of the water, the dark of the belly of the fish. No ship, no crew, no one to hear him. The man who walked out on his people in anger has nowhere left to walk. And in there, he says something.
screen: `THE DARK OF THE NIGHT.` → `THE DARK OF THE SEA.` → `THE DARK OF THE FISH.`

segments.voice: Surah Al-Anbiya says he cried out in the darkness, in Pickthall's translation: “There is no God save Thee. Be Thou glorified! Lo! I have been a wrong-doer.” In Arabic: la ilaha illa anta, subhanaka, inni kuntu mina z-zalimin. Three short pieces. First, la ilaha illa anta: there is no god but You. That's tawhid, day ten of this path, but said face to face. Not about Allah, to Him. Second, subhanaka: glory to You, above any fault. Third, and hardest: I was one of the wrongdoers. No excuse. He doesn't mention how stubborn his people were, or say they drove him to it. He says, I was wrong. You've heard that shape before on this path. Adam and Hawwa: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. Musa after the blow: my Lord, I have wronged myself. The prophets keep saying it. Then the next verse: “Then We heard his prayer and saved him from the anguish. Thus We save believers.” Not just Yunus: the Qur'an turns the story outward. A hadith in Tirmidhi says that whenever a Muslim calls with the prayer of Dhu n-Nun, for anything, it is answered. That's why so many Muslims know these words by heart, and say them in their own dark places: a hospital corridor, a pile of debt, three in the morning. Another surah adds that if Yunus had not been one who glorified Allah, he would have stayed in the belly of the fish until the day of rising.
screen: `LA ILAHA ILLA ANTA: NO GOD BUT YOU.` · `SUBHANAKA: GLORY TO YOU.` · `I HAVE BEEN A WRONG-DOER.` · `WE HEARD HIS PRAYER AND SAVED HIM.` · then, large: `THUS WE SAVE BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let it be dark. If you pray, say the prayer of Yunus slowly, three times, silently or in a whisper, with a breath between each piece: la ilaha illa anta, subhanaka, inni kuntu mina z-zalimin. If you don't pray, simply listen to the words in your mind and let the last one land: I was wrong, said without an excuse.
Three darknesses. The night, the sea and the fish, where Yunus called: there is no god but You, glory to You, I was wrong.
Your line: la ilaha illa anta, there is no god but You. Tomorrow, what happened when he came out. See you then.

screen: `DAY 76 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GOURD AND THE SAVED CITY.`

77.title: The gourd and the saved city
77.hook: Yunus is cast ashore, sick, and shaded by a gourd vine, and the people he walked away from turn back and are spared
77.tomorrow: Mecca, a valley of trade and idols
77.howItsDone: Muslims read the end of Yunus's story in Surah As-Saffat and Surah Yunus, and it is often recalled as a reminder that no one should despair of a people turning back to Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three darknesses, and Yunus's prayer from inside the fish. Your line was la ilaha illa anta: there is no god but You.

A bare shore. Allah cast him there while he was sick: the Qur'an tells it in a single line, and that's all it says. A man lying on the sand under a hard sun, weak, barely able to lift his head. No shade, no food, no one. The man who walked out on his people has nothing left at all. And then, right over him, something begins to grow: a vine with wide green leaves, spreading over his body like an umbrella. The Qur'an names the plant. It's a gourd.
screen: `A BARE SHORE, A SICK MAN.` → `NO SHADE, NO ONE.` → `A VINE BEGINS TO GROW.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation: “And We caused a tree of gourd to grow above him.” In Arabic, yaqtin. Commentators explain it as a fast-growing gourd with broad leaves, the kind that gives quick shade and keeps flies away from a sick man's skin. A small mercy, sized exactly to what he needed. Then the Qur'an turns to the part Yunus never saw coming: “And We sent him to a hundred thousand (folk) or more.” And they believed. The people he walked out on, the ones he was sure would never listen, turned back to Allah. Surah Yunus, the tenth surah, the one named for him, singles them out. It wishes aloud that the other towns warned of old had believed in time, as the people of Yunus did. When they believed, the punishment was lifted from them, and they were given enjoyment of life for a while. Commentators say the people went out together, men, women and children, and cried to Allah when they saw the warning signs, and they were spared. Yunus left because he was certain they wouldn't change. And they changed. In the Qur'an's stories of warned towns, this is the one the text holds up as turning around in time. And that closes week eleven: a messenger in the eastern place, a palm tree, a baby who spoke, Isa by Allah's leave, a man who left in anger, three darknesses, and a gourd vine over a city that believed.
screen: `A TREE OF GOURD ABOVE HIM.` · `A HUNDRED THOUSAND OR MORE.` · `THE TOWN THAT TURNED IN TIME.` · `HE WAS SURE. THEY CHANGED.` · then, large: `THE CITY BELIEVED.`

segments.voice: Think of something you walked away from, or someone you gave up on: a friendship, a project, a skill, a relative. Picture it now, without the old certainty that it would never change, and let the question sit: what if it has changed, or what if you have? If you pray, you can ask Allah to open the way.
Yaqtin, gourd: the vine that grew to shade sick Yunus, in the same story where the city he gave up on believed.
Your line: the city believed. Tomorrow, the stories of the prophets arrive in a valley called Mecca. Eleven weeks on the path.
